claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite contains discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The initial W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Introducing a trace or minor amount of Zr during co-sintering will selectively dope the W–Cu interfaces.
Zr preferentially migrates to and segregates at W–Cu interfaces during sintering.
Interfacial Zr segregation lowers the local W–Cu interfacial energy.
Interfacial Zr promotes better atomic coherence and bonding between W and Cu.
The Zr-mediated interface suppresses compositional phase separation.
The Zr-mediated interface inhibits interfacial void formation.
Reduced phase separation and void formation maintain a more continuous thermally conductive pathway.
Zr-doped W–Cu will have fewer interfacial voids than identically processed undoped W–Cu.
Zr-doped W–Cu will exhibit less phase separation than identically processed undoped W–Cu.
Zr-doped W–Cu will have higher overall thermal conductivity than undoped W–Cu under comparable irradiation and thermal loading.
Untreated W–Cu naturally develops phase separation and interfacial voids during high-temperature sintering.
Untreated W–Cu develops phase separation and interfacial voids under irradiation and thermal stresses in service.
Fusion divertor applications involve W-based plasma-facing materials, Cu-based cooling components, high thermal flux, and irradiation exposure.
A working-temperature mismatch between W plasma-facing material and CuCrZr cooling pipes motivates an interlayer between them.
The intervention is expected to work only within optimized co-sintering temperature–time profiles and may perform differently outside the stated thermal and irradiation regimes.
The quantitative conductivity improvement, long-term irradiation stability, optimal Zr concentration, and optimal sintering regime remain undetermined.
